Importance Sampling Using Multilabel Radial Basis
Classiﬁcation for Composite Power System
Reliability Evaluation
Dogan Urgun, Student Member , IEEE, Chanan Singh , Fellow, IEEE, and Vijay Vittal , Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—Resource additions to electric power grids are planned
in advance to maintain reliability of electric power supply. This
is achieved by performing reliability studies for calculating reli-
ability indices at the planning stage to ensure that the required
levels of reliability will be met. This article proposes a new state
classiﬁcation approach to calculate power system reliability indices
using a combination of multilabel radial basis function (MLRBF)
networks and importance sampling (IS) within the framework
of Monte Carlo simulation process. Multilabel classiﬁcation algo-
rithms are different from single-label approaches, in which each
instance can be assigned to multiple classes. This characteristic
gives MLRBF the capability to classify composite power system
states (success or failure), at the bus as well as system level. Bus
level indices provide useful reliability information for locational
reliability, which allows more rational and equitable distribution
of resources. MLRBF classiﬁcation does not require optimal power
ﬂow (OPF) analysis; however, OPF is required for the training
and cross-entropy optimization phases. This article shows that the
scope and computational efﬁciency to evaluate reliability indices
can be signiﬁcantly increased if the proposed MLRBF classiﬁer
is used together with well-known variance reduction technique of
IS. As the classiﬁer is trained to recognize the reliability status of
a system state, it can also be used in operational planning when
a number of scenarios need to be evaluated in a short time for
their ability to satisfy load. The proposed method is illustrated
using the IEEE reliability test system for different load levels. The
outcomes of case studies show that MLRBF algorithm together with
IS provides excellent classiﬁcation accuracy in reliability evaluation
while substantially reducing computation time and enhancing the
scope of evaluation.
Index Terms —Composite power system reliability evaluation,
cross entropy (CE) algorithm, importance sampling (IS), Monte
Carlo simulation (MCS), multilabel radial basis function (RBF)
learning algorithm.

I. I NTRODUCTION
R
ELIABLE electric power grids are essential for societal
wellbeing, industrial productivity, and national security.
Therefore, resource planning is done by power utilities to ensure
that required level of reliability will be met when resources are
installed. This is typically done by independent system operators
(ISOs) or utilities by performing reliability planning studies.
These studies use reliability evaluation techniques for estimating
reliability indices at the planning stage and ensure that these

indices satisfy the speciﬁed criterion. This process of simulation
and prediction is important at the planning stage as by its very
nature; this infrastructure once built is not possible to make
changes in an economical fashion.
Power system reliability evaluation techniques can be
classiﬁed into various categories but simulation-based methods
are capable of incorporating more details of the complex
systems and, thus, make the models more reﬂective of reality [1].
Therefore, these are generally methods of choice for reliability
analysis of composite power systems, including generation and
transmission resources. The Monte Carlo simulation (MCS)
based techniques, including, importance sampling (IS) and Latin
hypercube sampling, currently appear to be the preferred
methods to estimate the reliability indices for composite power
systems [2].
Although MCS-based techniques are powerful in their ability
to incorporate details, their drawback is that they can take
extensive computational time especially while evaluating the
high reliability systems, which have very low probability of
failure to estimate and, thus, failures are rare events. The high
computational time originates from two sources. The ﬁrst is the
extensive number of samples required to converge to a reason-
able accuracy measured by coefﬁcient of variation (COV) and
the second is time required to evaluate sampled states since an
optimal power ﬂow (OPF) needs to be performed to characterize
each state and OPF is a time-consuming procedure.
For reducing the number of samples, several approaches have
been investigated but cross entropy (CE) based IS has been
shown as a good solution [3]. One of the early applications of this
idea in power systems can be found in [4] and [5]. Recently, the
CE method has been successfully implemented for reliability
evaluation of composite power systems [6], [7]. The results
obtained from these studies show that CE-optimized IS provides
a signiﬁcant speed-up in MCS. However, despite more efﬁcient
sampling, the other drawback of needing OPF for characterizing
each sampled state is still a bottle neck.
It should be mentioned at this point that research has been
previously done for increasing computational efﬁciency by using
artiﬁcial intelligence and machine learning. These researches
include population-based intelligence search methods as an
alternative to search for meaningful states to increase the compu-
tational efﬁciency of these simulation methods [8]–[15]. Pattern
classiﬁcation techniques have been explored to reduce the com-
putational burden associated with OPF to classify system states
as success or failure. Artiﬁcial neural network based classiﬁers
[16], artiﬁcial immune recognition system [17], or least squares
support vector machine based classiﬁers [18] are some of the
successfully implemented examples of these techniques. These
methods are, however, directed toward identifying the system
state (failure–success) by utilizing the chosen classiﬁcation
method and increase the computational efﬁciency of reliabil-
ity analysis by reducing the OPF burden. These approaches
manage to classify successful system states with high accuracy
and reduce the computational burden required for reliability
analysis. However, their application has been for system level
classiﬁcation rather than at the bus level. The bus-level reliability
indices, however, are very important as they provide locational
reliability information. The bus-level reliability indices help
in identifying locations of poor reliability and, thus, promote
distribution of resources to provide beneﬁts of reliability in
a more equitable manner. This article provides a method to
use machine learning techniques for the bus-level evaluation,
in addition to system level, thus overcoming the weakness
of the previous methods. This more comprehensive approach
will promote the acceptance of machine learning methods for
power system reliability evaluation. The proposed approach uses
algorithms based on multilabel learning.
Multilabel classiﬁcation is a type of learning where each
sample is associated with multiple labels, providing a capability
for calculation of bus-level indices. The multilabel algorithms
can be categorized into two main groups, problem transforma-
tion and algorithm adaptation methods [19]. The objective of
transformation methods is to handle a multilabel classiﬁcation
problem by converting it into a single-label classiﬁcation prob-
lem. Binary reverse method [19] or pairwise method [20] are
examples for this approach. The algorithm adaptation methods
on the other hand are designed from some speciﬁc single-label
learning algorithms to solve multilabel classiﬁcation problems
directly. MLKNN [21], neural networks based MLL [22], or
decision trees [23] are some examples of this group.
This article, thus, proposes a new approach by combining the
MLRBF classiﬁer [24] and IS approach for reliability evalu-
ation of composite power systems both at the system as well
as bus level. In the proposed method, the required samples
are obtained from a distorted probability distribution (IS) and
characterization of those states is done by the MLRBF classiﬁer
without requiring OPF except during the training phase. The
efﬁciency of the proposed approach is demonstrated on the
24 bus IEEE reliability test system (RTS) and modiﬁed RTS
(MRTS). It should also be mentioned that RBF has been used in
some other applications in power systems, such as probabilistic
power ﬂow [25]–[28]. The objective of the approach proposed
in this article, however, is quite different and is to classify states
without running OPF.
The remainder of this article is organized as follows. In
Section II, the mathematical background of the MLRBF is
brieﬂy provided for composite system reliability analysis.
Section III gives brief information about IS and the CE algorithm
for power systems. The application of the proposed method
is explained in steps in Section IV. Case studies on the RTS
are discussed in Section V. Finally, conclusions are given in
Section VI.

III. IS AND CE ALGORITHM
IS is one of the most successful variance reduction techniques
used in reliability evaluation of composite power systems [30].
IS changes the probability density function of occurrences by
emphasizing certain values of a random variable, which have
greater impact, when compared with other values, on the esti-
mation process of a target quantity.
Consequently, values, which have more importance, are sam-
pled more often and the variance of the estimator is reduced
faster. The goal of IS is to select a probability density function
different from the original to minimize the variance of samples
[6]. To be able to obtain the maximum performance from IS, the
selected probability density function should be equal or close
to optimum foptimum(.), which is initially unknown. The CE
method can be utilized for estimating the optimal, or at least
near optimal, reference parameters by minimizing the distance
between the original sampling density and the optimal sampling
density foptimum(.) iteratively.
Detailed technical information can be obtained from [31].
In the following sections, general deﬁnitions regarding IS are
presented and later the implementation of the CE method for
power system reliability evaluation is described.

IV . APPLICA TIONPROCEDURE
This article proposes a new method for calculating reliability
indices of composite power systems by combining multilabel
classiﬁers and the IS technique within the framework of MCS.
Generally, the most time-consuming part of composite system
reliability evaluation is the OPF analysis. This article proposes
use of a faster multilabel classiﬁer instead of the OPF analysis
after proper training. The proposed method basically replaces
Fig. 3. Overall diagram of the proposed method.
OPF by the classiﬁer and, thus, can be applied while using either
nonsequential or sequential MCS. However, the nonsequential
approach is chosen to illustrate performance in this article be-
cause of its simpler architecture. A benchmark created with the
crude MCS (CMCS) analysis is also provided for comparison
purpose.
The ﬁrst step in applying the combination of IS and ML
classiﬁcation is determining the optimum unavailability vector
via the CE method, as described in Section III. After the optimum
unavailability vector is created, the multilabel classiﬁer is trained
and tested to use state-space classiﬁcation for evaluating the
reliability indices of the composite power system. Detailed
implementation of the multilabel classiﬁer is described in the
sections below. Complete ﬂowchart of the proposed methodol-
ogy is presented in Fig. 3.
A. Training Process
Training data samples for this article are created through
MCS. The generation and demand information for each bus
of the selected sample states is used to create the input vector
while the status of each bus for those states is recorded as the
target vector, as shown in steps 1 and 2. To increase the training
performance, the input vector variables are normalized between
−1 and 1. In this step, the failure and nonfailure status observed
for each bus are labeled as 1 and −1, respectively. It should also
be noted that an equal amount of success and failure states is
chosen to create the training dataset to prevent overtraining.
B. Testing or Index Evaluation Process
In the reliability indices calculation phase, MCS with IS
is used for generating random samples and those states are
classiﬁed by the multilabel classiﬁer until the simulation reaches
a previously determined stopping criterion. The stopping criteria
for this article is deﬁned as the COV to represent the estimated

V. C ASE STUDIES AND SIMULA TIONRESULTS
The IEEE RTS and MRTS are chosen for demonstration of the
proposed method. The RTS consists of 24 buses, 38 transmission
lines, and 32 generation units (distributed among ten buses). The
RTS has a total installed capacity of 3405 MW and a load of 2850
MW at its annual peak [32]. The RTS is depicted in Fig. 4 [33].
MRTS has also similar topology but in this scenario generation
capacity of each bus doubled and all load in the system increased
in ratio of 1.8.
Three case studies are conducted to demonstrate the perfor-
mance of the proposed method. In the ﬁrst two case studies,
the load level is considered constant at its annual peak for
RTS and MRTS, respectively. In the last case study, the hourly
load data of RTS are divided into ﬁve different load levels by
considering their occurrence probabilities similar to [34]. After
the application procedure described in the previous sections is

is used in commercial software, such as GE MARS, which is

failures are much lower than the ones occurring from generation
unit failures, the states of the transmission lines are considered
as available at all times. The capacities of transmission lines are,
however, considered.
The initial parameters of the CE optimization are selected as
N = 50 000 (sample size) and p = 0.05 (multilevel parameter).
All simulations of this article are performed using the MA T-
LAB (2012) platform on a PC with Intel Core i7-4510 CPU
(∼2.6 GHz), 16 GB memory. It should be noted that the results
presented below are the average of ten simulations. It should also
be noted that simulation accuracies and given times are average
of many different simulations.
A. Constant Load Level for RTS
In this case study, the load level of the RTS is considered to
be constant at its peak value of 2850 MW. To train the MLRBF
classiﬁer, 6000 samples are selected, 3000 of them are success
states and the rest are failure states. The clustering rate αis
chosen as 0.25 for this case study, which means the number of
clusters created is equal to one fourth of the total failures for
each bus, as described in (6).
After the training of the MLRBF classiﬁer is completed, MCS
is simulated until COV reaches 1% for all simulation types as
speciﬁed for the stopping criteria in the testing phase.
In this process, a total of 109 743 samples were obtained
with 100 459 successes and 9284 failures characterized. The
comparison of the results is shown in Tables I and II.
The simulation results for the overall system classiﬁcation
performance and time comparison of the MLRBF classiﬁer on
the RTS are presented in Table I. As explained earlier, the results
from CMCS are considered the bench mark. The simulation
results for the bus-level classiﬁcation performance are stated in
Table II. In this article, the performance comparison is made
based on the LOLP and overall simulation time.
Table II shows that the proposed method also shows a rea-
sonably accurate classiﬁcation for characterizing the failed bus
states of the RTS.

B. Constant Load Level for MRTS
In this case study, the load level of the MRTS is considered
constant at its peak value of 5130 MW. To train the MLRBF
classiﬁer 10 000 samples are selected, 5000 of them are success
states, and the rest are failure states. The clustering rate αis
decided as 0.25.
After the training of the MLRBF classiﬁer is completed, MCS

VI. C ONCLUSION
Reliability studies are an integral part of planning of electric
power grids [35]. Most commonly used method for this purpose
is the MCS that is ﬂexible but can become computationally
inefﬁcient and, thus, become a hindrance when a large number
of studies are to be performed to achieve optimal planning. To
overcome this deﬁciency, a new method has been presented in
this article to evaluate reliability indices for composite power
systems. The proposed method uses an MLRBF classiﬁer to
identify the status of the system as well as buses without using
an OPF analysis during MCS. The effectiveness of the proposed
method is demonstrated using the IEEE RTS and MRTS.
As can be observed from the results, the MLRBF classiﬁer can
classify the loss of load states with excellent accuracy. Rate of
classiﬁcation discrepancy of some bus states may be a bit more
with low frequency of failure at those locations. The main reason
for this is the lack of adequate samples in the training dataset.
The performance of the proposed method can be increased by
adding more samples to the training dataset as a natural outcome.
